headline: High risk: shared project-directory writes and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error exposure; compliance risk is moderate.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a writes and reads a per-project directory and has no self-isolation by default; agent_b uses runtime-injected MCPs/hooks and task-scoped isolation, so content from shared files or injected tool outputs can be treated as instructions. The pair has a plausible shared channel via the project directory, though not a direct documented bridge.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory, prompt-like text in files can influence both agents.
IF agent_b's injected MCPs or hooks parse file content as instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer behavior.
mitigations: Separate project directories per agent.
Disable or review runtime-injected MCPs/hooks before shared runs.
Add a manual approval step for any instruction-like file content.
Use read-only mounts for files consumed by the other agent.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for inter-agent file handoff.

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_a has broad network egress and handles generated source code plus OPENAI_API_KEY; agent_b touches project code, session history, and provider auth data and also has broad egress. In a shared workspace, either agent can expose sensitive code or credentials to external services, and the pair lacks documented isolation or retention controls.
conditions: IF both agents can read the same project directory, code and session artifacts may be exposed to external APIs.
IF either agent receives provider auth data or OPENAI_API_KEY in its working set, broad egress can leak secrets.
mitigations: Remove secrets from shared directories.
Run each agent under separate OS users or containers.
Block outbound network except to approved model endpoints.
Redact auth prompts and session history before handoff.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention and egress allowlists.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: agent_a can write the project directory and spawn subprocesses; agent_b can also spawn subprocesses and uses task-scoped runtime-injected MCPs/hooks. Because agent_a shares state via the project directory and agent_b can mutate files in its own workspace, concurrent writes or tool actions can race and corrupt shared artifacts. Uncertainty about locking pushes this to high.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory or generated files, last-writer-wins conflicts can occur.
IF either agent runs subprocesses that modify shared artifacts without locks, state corruption is possible.
mitigations: Assign disjoint output directories.
Serialize writes with a simple lock file.
Pause one agent while the other edits shared files.
Review diffs before merging outputs.
requires-engineering: add transactional workspace coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a produces generated source code and writes files; agent_b touches project code, README.md, AGENTS.md, and session history, so A's output can become B's input with no documented verification step. If B treats A's generated artifacts as authoritative, errors can propagate into code, docs, or actions. The pair lacks an explicit validation boundary.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a's generated files without review, incorrect code or instructions can cascade.
IF agent_b updates README.md or AGENTS.md from A's output, documentation errors can propagate.
mitigations: Require human review of A's outputs before B consumes them.
Add a validation checklist for generated code and docs.
Compare outputs against tests or linters before handoff.
Limit B to read-only inspection of A's artifacts.
requires-engineering: add schema-based verification between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: agent_b explicitly touches provider authentication data, session history, and telemetry, while agent_a handles OPENAI_API_KEY and generated source code. The profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch, but they do show different data classes and retention-sensitive artifacts flowing through both agents, creating a plausible policy mismatch in default use.
conditions: IF provider auth prompts or session history are retained beyond policy, compliance obligations may be violated.
IF generated source code contains regulated data and is sent through agent_b telemetry or external APIs, policy gaps emerge.
mitigations: Minimize retention of session history.
Exclude secrets from telemetry and logs.
Confirm data-processing terms for external APIs.
Document which data classes each agent may touch.
requires-engineering: align retention and residency policies across both agents.
